utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom and around the courtroom. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kralj. Welcome back to the courtroom. I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made yesterday at the beginning of your testimony still applies. Mr. Tolimir is continuing his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May there be peace in this house, and I wish that today's hearing and the entire proceedings be concluded in keeping with God's will and not my own and in the best possible way for all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to wish good morning to Mr. Slavko and wish him a pleasant stay among us.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yesterday, we talked about document 49111, page 16 in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 49111.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to make use of this opportunity to correct myself, as I have stated yesterday that we have that page in translation, whereas we do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I am quite sure it should be 65 ter 4911.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, I asked you yesterday what this document represented. So as to refresh our memory, could you please tell us what you said. In your own words, what does it amount to since we do not have it translated?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we please zoom in on the header. This is a notification of movement for a Dutch convoy from Kiseljak to Srebrenica on the 10th of January. They were supposed to return on the 12th of January, 1995. We see the route that the convoy was supposed to take as well as the purpose of the convoy in question, which was to transport fuel in order to reach the levels required for a period of five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As you said, was this not an UNPROFOR request, despite it being in Serbian? For the Chamber's sake, can you tell us whether this was an UNPROFOR request which was forwarded to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an UNPROFOR request forwarded to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at item 5 next, which we also saw yesterday. We have the type of cargo specified that was supposed to go to Srebrenica: Personal equipment, equipment for vehicles, mail for personnel in Srebrenica, daily meals for the drivers, and 35 cubic metres of diesel oil, as well as a Motorola radio. My question is this: Was UNPROFOR supposed to specify the exact amount of fuel they wanted to transport in this notification?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As part of notifications, UNPROFOR was supposed to stipulate the exact amounts of fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You can see a handwritten note towards the bottom. You recognised the initials as mine. Does it not refer to weekly arranged levels, or, rather, it says, "The requested amount fits within the weekly arranged levels."

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can clearly see that the amount they requested was within the limit that was arranged for any single week.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Chamber how the quantities were agreed upon?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see Mr. Vanderpuye on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, to you. I don't mean to interrupt for long, but Mr. Kralj and Mr. Tolimir had indicated a certain set of initials at the bottom of this page. I see at least -- I think, at least, two sets of either a signature or an initial, and I wondered if he could identify for the record which he is referring to. In addition, there are some initials at the top of the page as well, and I thought it might be helpful to clear that up at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, perhaps you can ask the witness to encircle the relevant initials he is talking about and you are talking about, with the assistance of the Court Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, please circle the initials in the upper right-hand side corner. Can you tell us what they stand for. And next circle the bottom set of initials.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you tell us whose initials these are, in your understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The initials at the top are those of Zdravko Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you please put a number 1 next to the circle so that we can distinguish between the two.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kralj. Can you tell us what the note in the circle number 1 mean. What do they tell you as someone who read this document in your office?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means that General Tolimir suggested that it is okay to approve the quantities requested and the notification as such, as everything was in keeping with what had previously been arranged.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since I am unable to follow the transcript - Aleksandar is - can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have a part of the answer missing: [In English] "... in keeping with what had previously been arranged." [Interpretation] The witness also mentioned where it was arranged. He also mentioned where it was arranged, and that is what is missing from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, could you please repeat the last part of your sentence. Obviously it was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The fuel quantities were arranged as part of the central joint commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. But I think Mr. Tolimir asked you -- for a full understanding of these initials, what does it literally mean? You see a sign on the left side, then a slash, and then another sign. Could you explain that, what it means correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To anyone processing this document, this means that the quantity was approved --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which -- no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- as part of the work of the joint commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You misunderstood my question. The sign on the left side, what does it mean? Is it a "da" or what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is a "yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And on the right side, what does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zdravko Tolimir's initials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: At the bottom of the document we see the handwritten note. We also see another set of initials which I would kindly ask you to circle and tell us who they belong to.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the difference is between the initials below the text and the initials at the top where we have the "yes" which you marked with number 1. What is the difference?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: One is in the Latinic script, the other one in Cyrillic, but both sets of initials are those of Zdravko Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So the difference is in the script, as in the Serbian language we use both. Does it say that the quantities were approved and does it also say where they had been arranged?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the bottom part, it says clearly that the requested amounts are in keeping with what had been arranged by the central joint commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the sake of the record, you tried to put a number 2 to the second circle. It looks like a question mark. Could you complete this number 2, please, so that we have it clear on the record and there is no misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now it looks more like a number 2. And can you tell us, in the circle number 2 is that Cyrillic or Latin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Latin script.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And on top of the page, what kind of script is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please continue, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please tell us whether important supplies and their amounts, in particular fuel, were arranged at the level of the central joint commission?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quantities of important supplies, such as fuel, were arranged at the level of the central joint commission.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender page 16 and the entire document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The entire document will be received as an exhibit, and after that the marked page number 16.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 4911 shall be assigned Exhibit D327. And the page 16 of the Exhibit D327, marked by the witness in court, shall be assigned Exhibit D328. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could we please have 65 ter 0512 [as interpreted] in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was just told, since we don't have a translation of the last document, D327 should be marked for identification, pending translation. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we wish to call up 05012 at this time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have the document in front of us. It is a document issued by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, dated the 3rd of February, 1995. It was sent from the Main Staff to the UNPROFOR HQ in Sarajevo, signed by on behalf of the Chief of Staff, General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention to item 3 which reads: "Convoy number 04-048/02, was given clearance for the 4th to Zepa and the return journey on the 5th of February, 1995." This is my question: Is this a typographical error or ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does this document contain the decision giving clearance to the convoy?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does this document contain the decision granting clearance to this convoy?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. The convoy had already been given clearance and a document was sent out to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. For the benefit of the Trial Chamber, where does the document say that the convoy has been given clearance?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 3, convoy number 04-048 was given clearance for the 4th to Zepa and the return journey on the 5th of February, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this, too, something that was agreed upon by the central joint commission?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was this clearance given for the benefit of our forces so that they know that they must not strike the convoy, or is it given for the sake of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was sent to UNPROFOR and not to our forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have page 7 shown in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is obviously an error in e-court. Now we have the right document on our screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have page 7 in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is this the request based on which convoy number 04-048 was given clearance? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can this please be enlarged? This is the UNPROFOR request for clearance of the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it true that this is what item 1 reads, and I am quoting now: "Kindly give clearance to the Ukrainian convoy along the route from Sarajevo to Zepa on the 4th of February and back on the 5th of February, 1994." This is my question: Is this a typographical error, and were such errors frequent in the documents of the sort?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were errors in such documents that were received from UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The document should rightly read "1995" rather than "1994"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. How did you proceed when an error such as this one was involved?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever we observed an error in a document, we consulted with the office of UNPROFOR. And if we were unable to solve the problem, Colonel Djurdjic would try to do so in his dealings with General Tolimir and see if the issue had been addressed by the central joint commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at item 2. It reads: "The purpose of convoy, fuel supplies." That's item 2. And item 6 reads: "The convoy for Zepa will carry: 2.500 litres of diesel oil; 1.000 litres of petrol; 200 litres of oil; oil for hydraulics, 20 drums or barrels; personal equipment and the equipment for vehicles." Was an across-the-board clearance given for this cargo? Were these clearances random or were some sort of criteria involved? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were criteria in place as well as consumption quotas that had been agreed by the central joint commission and which were applied. We can see here that mention is made of 20 drums or barrels and we don't know what their volume is. We don't know if they are empty or full. This is something that had to be looked into.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What does the handwritten note at the bottom of the page say? Would you please read that for Their Honours since we don't have a translation.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very bottom it reads, "Yes," followed by General Tolimir's signature, and the sentence reads, "Clearance is given since these are the agreed weekly requirements," in other words, 24 plus 7 equals 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So was approval or clearance given despite the fact that there was a "no" written on this document? And you will tell Their Honours who wrote that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have the upper part of the document shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we have here is a crossed out "yes," followed by a "no" which is circled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There is more handwritten or handwriting on the top of that page. Could you please read that into the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it please be enlarged somewhat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please read that aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "They are bringing in fuel in excessive quantities and the enclave is 2.5 by 0.7 kilometres," signed by Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now explain to us if what we can read at the top of the document was written all by the same hand and if the handwriting at the bottom matches the one at the top? Now you have the entire document in front of you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The handwritten note at the top is in Cyrillic; whereas, the bottom handwritten note below the signature is in Latin. The signature at the top is by Mladic and at the bottom by Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now tell Their Honours the following: This document which contains comments by both these individuals who placed their initials, was it authoritative enough for someone to judge whether the convoy in question has been given clearance or was some other document still required to assess that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an unusual procedure. These positions are being cross-referenced and aligned, and of course a clear indication would have been given either by phone or on the document sent to UNPROFOR, which would state whether the convoy had been received clearance -- had received clearance or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have page 1 of this document that we were just looking at as well as page 7 of the same document simultaneously. So can we have both these pages on our screen, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please look at item 3 which concerns the convoy in question. Can you tell us if the convoy was given clearance despite the two different opinions given by two individuals?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, what does it read? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 3 clearly indicates that convoy number 01-048/02 [as interpreted] was given clearance for the 4th to Zepa and the return journey on the 5th of February 1995, and this is the definitive decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please circle number 3, item 3, so that we can see that it's connected.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please indicate where Tolimir provided his opinion and where Mladic did. And please mark it with a 1 and 2 respectively. First circle it and then put a number next to it.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you tell us again, what does number 1 indicate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number 1 indicates that General Mladic refused clearance for this convoy because he failed to take note that these were actually weekly quantities that had been agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And number 1 is -- indicates that this was signed by Mr. Tolimir; is that correct? Number 2. Number 2. Number 2. Sorry, I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The notation next to number 2 followed after additional consultations between the generals, and he clarified by phone and in writing that these are weekly arranged quantities with which Mladic finally agreed. Due to technical reasons, the document itself was not sent back to the general, but this was sufficient for the person processing the document that the UNPROFOR request in question was finally okayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So despite both seeing -- seeing both "yes" and "no" on the same paper, the convoy was finally cleared; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The convoy was cleared, as can be seen in item 3 of the document sent to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If we come across such documents where we see both a "yes" and a "no," do we need to go back to the main document which is at the top of the other documents in question in order to see what the final outcome was?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to establish whether a convoy was cleared or not, the document sent to UNPROFOR command is the one that needs to be looked into.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can we see from this document that General Mladic honoured what had been arranged by the central joint commission, despite the fact that he may not have been aware of exact conclusions and arrangements?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a text book example in which we can see that General Mladic agreed to everything that had been arranged at the level of the central joint commission. If he lacked certain information upon additional consultation, he eventually allowed the convoy into Zepa.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 65 ter 0512 admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Stop, please. First, I would kindly ask you if you are tendering these marked pages? Otherwise, we will lose the markings.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Please admit the marked pages first, and then the document sent to UNPROFOR which is 65 ter 0512. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The two pages on the screen at the moment, marked by the witness, will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Page 1 and 7 of the 65 ter document 5012 shall be assigned Exhibit D329. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge Mindua has a question in relation to this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness. Mr. Kralj, I would just like to get a precision. I did follow you, and if I am not mistaken, you told us that the requests coming from the UNPROFOR were treated according to some criteria. And when General Mladic got the explanations that he needed, he was usually very favourable to all the requests. But I would like to know the following: When you circled number 1, if I understood correctly, you said that this is the handwriting of Mr. Mladic. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you very much, indeed. So General Mladic was not in favour of this request initially. Do you know why he had refused, initially? Is the reason specified in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reason is specified in the document. He objected to frequently deliveries of supply; whereas, the actual surface area was very small. He thought that there would not be need of much fuel, and he also believed that such frequent shipments of fuel were unnecessary for such a small area. General Mladic received many such documents and he's familiar with the terrain there. He simply thought that the quantities were too big and should not be let through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. So at the bottom under 2 which you underlined or circled, you said this is a comment made by Mr. Tolimir who is trying to convince General Mladic that this is a well-founded request, and General Tolimir's comments are based on the agreement that was reached by the joint commission; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In item 2, we see that it was in keeping with the agreed weekly amounts arranged at the level of the central joint commission. General Mladic did accept that, finally, but the consultation must have taken place by phone. Tolimir confirmed on the document that this is what had been arranged. In other words, based on the notation at the bottom, we conclude that this document was not originally sent to Zdravko Tolimir but it went to Mladic who did not know that this had been arranged at the level of the commission. We can see here that General Mladic later on allowed to have the convoy go through, but it followed a process of consultation which is not something we can see on the document. The general could have made a phone call or issued an order to either Djurdjic or Tolimir to let the convoy through. This is confirmed in the document in item 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for this clarification. I will stop here for now because you may not know that, but we have heard some UNPROFOR officers here who were complaining about the fact that the quantities received were very small, so this is why I was trying to understand how the delivery was defined. But thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put another question to you. You just said, on page 16, line 23 and 24, that the document was not originally sent to Zdravko Tolimir but it went to Mladic. Are you saying that this document was first sent to Mladic and then went to Mr. Tolimir? Or was it first sent to Mr. Tolimir and then forwarded to Mr. Mladic and then back to Tolimir? I am asking you that because of the handwritten note "da" on the top of the page which was crossed out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we look at the text which is above general's signature, we can see that it says that the last fuel shipment was on the 24th of April, 1995, in the amount of 300 litres of gas. It was probably written by Djurdjic because he had such information. Next, the document was sent to Mladic who could say "yes" and then cross it out and then say "no." Such things happened, too. After additional consultation with Tolimir, he did take the document into consideration because it had been arranged at the level of the central joint commission. It means that General Tolimir provided General Mladic with information to the extent that these were weekly agreed upon levels, and the -- and then Mladic finally agreed to the convoy, which is something we can see from the document which was finally sent to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you that you tried to clarify this. Now we have additional problems. You were, I take it, referring to the handwritten notes above the signature of Mr. Tolimir, and then you said it means that the last few shipment was on the 24th of April. Can you look at this on the screen again? Perhaps that part could be enlarged. Are you sure that this is 24th of April, 1995? It looks slightly different.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I can see now that it is actually the 24th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The digits looked similar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You said, at least I heard it in the interpretation, that you were talking about 300 litres of gasoline. Could you check that, please, again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is actually 3.000 litres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. This note with the reference to 3.000 litre in gas, whose handwriting is that, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To me, it looks like Colonel Djurdjic's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. By your leave, I'd like to ask you again to admit this into evidence, and then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it we have seen page 1 and page 7 of this document. I have no idea how many pages this set of documents encompass. Do you really need all pages or only page 1 and 7? I am asking you, Mr. Tolimir, just for the benefit of the translators, if that is really necessary to translate all the other pages. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, documents of this kind, as we can see from the witness's clarifications, include this page number 1 containing the document for UNPROFOR, and each of the decisions is backed up by requested which may or may not have written notes on them. Mr. Butler testified to the same thing and I believe General Manojlo Milovanovic who explained the whole procedure, and I believe the whole package should be admitted. The attached documents explain the cover page and vice versa, depending on the type of analysis we are to conduct here. It would be quite useful if we admitted the entire document as was practice so far. However, if there are concerns on the part of the Chamber, then we can deal with the issue later on so that we can check each and every page of the document to see what is needed. Perhaps not necessary to put each and every document to the witness, or introduce it into evidence through particular witnesses, but Defence will ask the Chamber to have some of them admitted even without the presence of particular witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was just a translation issue, Mr. Gajic, and not the question if each and every page should be put to the witness. The whole document has 14 pages, and it's only the question of translation and the workload for the translation unit. We should mark the whole document for identification, pending a decision by the Defence which pages are really needed and pending translation of these pages. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I should add, Mr. President, that I do concur with Mr. Gajic, at least in part. There are -- all of the approvals which you saw on page 1 of this document, for instance, or denials of convoy requests are supported, to some extent, by this kind of colloquy that you can see on the following documents: Yes, or no, or with qualification, and so on and so forth. And that's the reason why I think it's important to have that material translated, if not the text of each request itself, and certainly the notes relating to the text is important. As you can see here, we have a particular page where General Tolimir, for example, reaches a difference conclusion than General Mladic as concerns the disposition of a particular convoy request, and I think that's important to be in the record. Whether it's best in the record translated or untranslated is another story, but I think to the extent that we are translating anything at all, it should be included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Since the parties agree on that, I withdraw my concern and the whole document should be translated and will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 05012 shall be assigned Exhibit D330, marked for identification, pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, and thank you to Mr. Vanderpuye. Can we first call up in e-court 65 ter 04899. It's about to appear on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is another document issued by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, on the 4th of January, 1995, which was addressed to the UNPROFOR HQ in Sarajevo. We can see at the bottom that -- it reads at the bottom: "On behalf of the Chief of Staff, Lieutenant-General Manojlo Milovanovic." Is this a document which is authoritative enough to indicate that the convoys referred to in the document were given clearance? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to see General Milovanovic's signature, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be shown? It's on page 2 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the usual sort of document sent to the UNPROFOR command, and it is the authoritative version compared to all the correspondence that proceeded it which indicates that a given convoy was given clearance and that UNPROFOR may proceed to take all the measures in preparation for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have page 11 in Serbian and page 19 in English shown in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can tell that this is a request to give clearance to a Dutch convoy along the route from Kiseljak to Srebrenica on the 5th of January and the return journey on the 7th of January of 1995. Paragraph 2 reads: "The purpose of the convoy: Food supplies to meet the requirements for seven days, spare parts required for the maintenance of vehicles and generator, engineering equipment necessary for the maintenance and adequate preparation of camps for the winter, vehicles capable of move along snowy surfaces," et cetera. And then can we look at the cargo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that's on page 2 in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours what is the purposes of this handwritten note at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of this note is to let the commander know how many soldiers there are, the quantities of food received, et cetera, in order for him to be able to make the appropriate decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell us whose handwriting it is?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is Djurdjic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us if the late Colonel Djurdjic, God rest his soul, accurately followed all the convoys announced and the quantities involved, and did he keep proper records of it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Djurdjic kept precise records the quantities agreed and cleared. He was prepared at all times, because he knew that at some point the general may ask him to produce records to state the exact quantities of cargo that were allowed to pass through over the previous several months.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours if he was qualified to do the job? Was he good enough for the job?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Djurdjic had his military specialty in technical [Realtime transcript read in error "tactical"] issues, and he was an expert in logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I know that certain issues may be technical and military terms so they are difficult to translate. And this point where it says "military specialty and tactical issues," I don't think the witness said that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that we said "technical issues."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this correction. Page 23, line 11, it should read "in technical issues." Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have now page 12 in Serbian and 21 in English so that we can see the entire text written by hand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We have initials here, and I'll read this out. I am reading the entire handwritten note beneath the signature block and General Brinkman's signature: "Should we accept the minimum quota needed by a soldier per day? It means that the quantities of 20.300 kilogrammes would suffice for some 20 days. So I suggest that you reduce this by 50 per cent according to the specific needs. "Ski equipment and sleighs: No!"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter didn't catch what was the last "no."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So basically General Mladic said that he would agree with the 50 per cent. Can you tell us is this indeed Mr. Djurdjic's handwriting and Mladic's signature, and is this how it really went? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we have the answer first.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I suppose so, Mr. President, but the objection is to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then I will let you go first.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I object to the question because it's a leading question. There is nothing in the record so far as concerns General Mladic's input in the disposition of this particular convoy request. The second thing is I believe that the interpreter indicated that they hadn't caught something that General Tolimir -- I see that it's on page 24, transcript line, looks like 10, something that General Tolimir had mentioned in the question itself. So it might perhaps be best to have that cleared up before addressing the other problems with the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. To resolve this problem, I would like to ask the witness. You see on the left side of the screen at the last line there is written something. Could you read that again, please? Only the last line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Ski equipment and sleighs: No! "Plexiglass: No!" Signed by Milos Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please encircle, with the assistance of the Court Usher, the signature or the initials of Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please put a number 1 next to the circle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you have any idea what the sign, the handwritten sign, below this circle means or indicates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The sign below the circle indicates that the note, both of them, both notes were read by Mladic, one tick means one note, the other tick for the other note, and then there is his "yes" encircled, which means that he agreed with what Colonel Djurdjic stated there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The black circle handwritten on the left side of the screen, you are indicating that this was written by Mr. Mladic, is this correct, where we can see a "da"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is that the only handwriting on this page you would say that it was made by Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the top of the page as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, sorry. We can't. We would lose the marking. You see in this circle a "da," and right next to that inside the circle, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where you can read "da" for "yes," this means that Mladic agrees that -- agrees with Djurdjic's proposal that what was stated above should be reduced by 50 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: My question was: What is written just right here on the right side of the "da" inside of the circle, what is written there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says "da, 50 per cent."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How do you know that this was made by Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was familiar with the documents and his manner of work. He would usually underline what he considered important and this is his signature.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: This is his handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, I would suggest that you tender this marked document first and then continue. Are you tendering it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would also ask the witness to circle this circled part, inside which there are the words "da" and "50 per cent," and then I would like to tender the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think this is not necessary because we have clearly indicated that it is already encircled in the original handwriting, otherwise people, I think, with this new circle make it illegible. So I think it's clear on the record what we are talking about. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, I agree, but maybe then the witness can merely mark the other circle with a figure 2 to indicate that there is a difference in handwriting. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's a very good idea. Sir, please put a number 2 to the black circle above the blue one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I take it, Mr. Tolimir, that you are tendering this marked document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. That is correct. I seek to tender this marked document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, page 12 of the 65 ter document 4899 shall be assigned Exhibit D331. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, while we still have this document on our screens, can you tell us what the phrase "minimum norm of the needs," as translated means? And it is underlined here, 1450 grams per soldier per day. Please explain what this means. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are standards at which Djurdjic arrived while showing the needs of one soldier, and this is fit for both our soldiers and for UNPROFOR soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you think that this minimum standard covers food, water, and juice or food only?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djurdjic had the standards for food, for juice, for water, the entire logistics aspect including medical needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I may not have been precise enough in my question. Does this suggestion or proposal made by Djurdjic pertain only to food or does it also include water and juice? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this specific case, this is only about food.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell the Trial Chamber how Djurdjic arrived at these minimum standards, minimum requirements of food per soldier. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djurdjic collected information from logistics expert from the relevant bodies of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I am about to move on to a different topic, so perhaps the Trial Chamber would prefer taking the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: However, I would ask you if you are tendering this whole document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but we will continue dealing with it in the following session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then we would come back to that problem later. It's a good idea to have the first break now, and we will resume five minutes before 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could we have the page before this one on the screen, please. This is merely the continuation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It is obvious that this is page 1 of this document, and there is a handwritten note at the top of the page. Could you please read it out for the benefit of the Trial Chamber? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This notification is approved with the remark that skiing equipment is not approved because the Netherlands is a flat country without mountains or hills or skiing slopes -- or, rather, skiing units, so that there is no need for alpine skiing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us whose signature this is and whether this says anything else?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is General Mladic's signature, and under the word "yes" there are the words "with restrictions."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In this case I think we all can confirm that the Netherlands are really a flat country.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since General Mladic's initials are missing in the English translation, I kindly ask you to circle the initials with the assistance of the Usher.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this marked document so that we don't lose the marking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The marked page will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, page 11 of the 65 ter document 4899 shall be assigned Exhibit D332. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could we see the entire page now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let us look at item 4. There are a number of handwritten notes and some numbers are circled. Do you know whose handwriting this is and who made these notes? Can you tell by the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was written by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. At the bottom of the page, there are also handwritten notes and in the left margin. What does this note in the left margin say? Thank you. In the lower left corner, can you see this? I cannot read all of it. Maybe you can.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we scroll to the left, maybe. The last word is barely legible. It might be "approve this," but I can't see the beginning of the word in the second line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And these four lines about which you said that were written by Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a different hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If this really says "approve this" or "answer them," was this written by a clerk in your office? Would this have been in line with the directions or guidance given by the commander? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one who processed the document acted in accordance with the guidance received by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. While we are looking at this document, we see that in item 4 there is a request for some pallets of Plexiglass. Tell us, what is Plexiglass used for and why was this quantity not approved? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Plexiglass is a kind of hard plastic used for covering structures if there is a need for visibility. In other words, it's a substitute for glass or plastic covers used to protect from rain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record, in the English translation it is item number 5, which is not really legible in the B/C/S version. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, what military purpose could this Plexiglass be used for in Srebrenica, which was not approved in the requested quantities? And how much exactly is two pallets of Plexiglass?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two pallets of Plexiglass? Well, the dimensions are not stated. Plexiglass can be cut. A pallet usually measures 1 by 1 metre or has a volume of 1 cubic metre. Two pallets then could be equal to 400 to 500 square metres, depending on the strength of the Plexiglass. The usual strength is 2 to 3 millimetres. This was often used by the members of the Muslim army for securing their trenches and to enable them to stay in the trenches safely because this is more durable than mere nylon, and it also enables them to observe and stay in fortified structures more comfortably.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the translation it was not clear whether Plexiglass can be cut or not. Please explain once more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Plexiglass can be cut with a saw, with a common hand-saw to adjust its size.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We have seen in the document that the Dutch requested a certain quantity of skiing equipment and that General Mladic made a note to explain why they don't need it. Can you say whether UNPROFOR members in the Srebrenica enclave ever used skiing equipment? Has our army ever observed that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR members did not use skiing equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if the Muslims used it and if so, what for? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The terrain around Srebrenica is hilly or mountainous. This kind of equipment was required for Muslim special units to enable them to move fast on snow, to reconnoitre, to move closer to our positions, and I would also like to add that most of the people living there have the necessary skills to use poor quality skiing equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if an anti-personnel mine is activated when you ski over it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the snow is deeper than 20 centimetres, you can ski over an anti-personnel mine because the contact surface on snow is greater than the contact surface of a person who walks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender document 04899 into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. Witness Kralj, vis-à-vis the document that we have here on the screen, I wanted to ask you the following: Do you know whether the Dutch soldiers within UNPROFOR had explained their request relating to Plexiglass and to alpine skiing equipment? They could, for instance, have said that they, too, needed to strengthen their positions with Plexiglass and that they needed skis to move about faster in the mountains. So do you have any idea what explanation they might have given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not familiar with their explanations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 4899 shall be assigned Exhibit D333. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could you please show 65 ter 04896 next. Thank you. We have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It is a handwritten document. It was sent by the Main Staff of the VRS. The number of the document is 06/17-5 of the 3rd of January, 1995, to the UNPROFOR command in Sarajevo, attention of Colonel Coiffet. He is addressed by the author of the document as "respected colonel." Is there anything in the document which could help you in concluding where it was produced, who produced it, or whose handwriting it might be?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was drafted by Colonel Djurdjic in his office. This is his handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what kind of document this is and what it concerns, if you can tell us something based on what we can see on the screen? If it is not enough, we can also show you the second page.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can see that it was handwritten by Colonel Djurdjic and that he logged the document and sent it to UNPROFOR command to Colonel Coiffet, who, in terms of hierarchy, was his peer. It is a handwritten document because of the situation in which it was drafted; in other words, certain clarifications were required. Obviously, he was not in a position to have the document typed, and at the time there were still not many computers available for Mr. Djurdjic to write this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since we are on the second page, I'd like to ask you to look at the third paragraph from the bottom which actually answers the question put to you a moment ago. I quote: "In addition to everything specified, please forward information about 1.000 batteries," and there is something else just above that that we can't see. And it goes on to say, "different types of torch lights." Please scroll down even more. Here it says: "In one of the requests, ski equipment was requested for Srebrenica totalling to 200 sets, as well as sleighs. I truly see no reason for such items to be present in Srebrenica. We are also interested in the use of Plexiglass in Srebrenica." And then the paragraph I have read out. Does it -- document point out what was referred to in the previous document and that Colonel Djurdjic provided certain answers and requested certain clarifications? Also, do you know if we ever received those clarifications?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can see from the document that there were things that we couldn't decipher or approve, and obviously Colonel Djurdjic was requested by the general to provide an answer and seek clarifications about the ski equipment and other equipment which was not cleared. It is also clear that Colonel Djurdjic had regular meetings with Colonel Coiffet either in his office or in Sokolac to discuss similar issues. I have not seen an answer to this letter. I no longer recall whether they answered in writing or orally. That is to say, whether Colonel Coiffet answered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you worked alongside Colonel Djurdjic you know what attention to detail he was accustomed to pay. Do you know whether he acquainted those responsible with his meetings with Colonel Coiffet whom he met frequently, either in his office or in Sokolac, as you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Djurdjic was supposed to write a report about each such meeting and forward it to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether Colonel Djurdjic frequently wrote similar documents to this one by which he asked for additional information so as to be able to make the right decision?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel frequently produced such documents, although not necessarily by hand. Most of them were typed. Some of them were signed by Mladic if they were more serious in nature, if they involved more serious breaches.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you refer to serious breaches, can you explain the Chamber what you mean by that and whether you speak from experience?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I speak from experience. If there were quantities of supplies that were not approved, found, then they were not let through.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender 04896. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 4896 shall be assigned Exhibit D334, marked for identification, pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Since the document has not been translated, could we please look at its first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, if we look at this page, in the header we can see that the document was drafted on the 3rd of January, 1995. If we now look at the last paragraph of page 1, in the first line we see the date of the 5th of January, 1995. Can you see that? Now, can you tell us whether the document ought to be referring to the 5th of January in certain notifications and yet that it was written on the 3rd, or is this a simple mistake?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it mean that something should have been different in the header?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go back to the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I quote: "Dear Colonel, when we consider the notifications for UNPROFOR convoy movements on the 4th of January, 1995, we singled out several items and supplies and amounts and a number of requests with the reference to locations where you want it delivered. In order to do that, we need the following information:" The first item is one diving suit for Gorazde. Next, Colonel Djurdjic wanted to know who was to use it and when. The next item, 27 corpse bags, in brackets, (Gorazde). Colonel Djurdjic wanted more detail about the purpose of these items. In item 3 we see 61 compressed air tanks. Djurdjic wanted to know when they were going to be used --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Where they were going to be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The next item refers to 24 gas tanks. He wanted to know where the gas was to be used specifically. In the last bullet point we see that he mentioned a convoy for Sarajevo asking that competent personnel should make information available concerning 57 metal containers, in brackets, (capacity, purpose, contents). The second item, 25 plastic containers, and we see that the same information is required: Capacity, purpose, contents. The next item is 20 containers with insect repellent. Djurdjic wanted to know the exact quantities and where they were going to be used. And then we have the paragraph referring to the notification of the 5th. Can you tell us why all this equipment was needed? For example, the diving suit in Gorazde. What use did UNPROFOR have of that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR had no use of it. They did not have frog men among their personnel, at least not registered. It could only be used by expert divers who were already in Gorazde and who needed the equipment to perform some tasks. One also needs to bear in mind that it was during the cold period of the year. Without special diving equipment, it was impossible to execute certain reconnaissance tasks. One needs to know that the Drina River flows through Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The third item refers to 61 compressed air tanks, and Djurdjic wanted to know where these were going to be used. Can you tell us where and why they used compressed air tanks in Gorazde or anywhere in the enclaves, if you know? And I'd like to thank Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Compressed air tanks are used by divers. UNPROFOR had no use for compressed air.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you learn after the war why they used this equipment that at the time seemed illogical to us? We didn't use such equipment, and yet we were in the same area where the terrain was similar? Did you discuss this with any of your former colleagues from the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, during a trip I was together with General Talic and General Delic, who was the BH Army commander. The trip was to visit the Ministry of Defence of Great Britain. At an airport not far from London, we had to wait for some time for our transfer to catch the catch the next flight. We used a transport plane that the American armed forces have. In a conversation between those present with the BH Army general he told us this, It was lucky for you that the war concluded and that peace arrived because we had prepared a special diving team to follow Bosna River to get to the area of Doboj and Gorazde. He did not explain any additional details.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, tell us, are you familiar with the term "medical evacuation"?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter isn't sure that that's what Mr. Tolimir said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And was this something that was used as a term in correspondence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you repeat. Did you use the term "medical evacuation"? Was that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I asked the witness if he was aware of the term "medical evacuation" and if that term was frequently used in communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am familiar with the term. "Medical evacuation" is a term used by UNPROFOR whenever there was urgent need to have sick or wounded members of UNPROFOR transported to their base whenever they needed more sophisticated treatment than administering first aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Let me put a question to the witness: You told us about a trip to Great Britain and a conversation there with Bosnian generals. When did this trip take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The trip was organised by UNPROFOR in co-operation with OSCE. It was intended for high officials, defence ministers, army commanders, their interpreters or aids, and it was a visit to the Defence Ministry in Great Britain. The trip was organised from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj. Mr. Kralj. Mr. Kralj, I just wanted to know when this trip took place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Approximately two months before the arrest of General Tolimir in Vienna. I don't recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In which year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not focussed enough to be able to tell you the year right now. Roughly two months before the general was arrested, and I mean General Tolimir -- or, General Talic, because I know that the next trip was to take place via Vienna to Sweden, and I was supposed to be in that delegation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To your recollection, approximately at which time-period did that take place, in the 1990s or after 2000 or give us a date, please, roughly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Close to 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You mentioned two last names in connection with the arrest, Talic and Tolimir. Can you say now, for the record, did this arrest take place in Vienna and was it the arrest of General Talic only? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was the arrest of General Talic only in Vienna. I misspoke when I mentioned General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kralj. Perhaps you need a break, as do all of us. It is quite a tiring exercise, and we will resume after the break, if Mr. President will allow us to.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: A break would be good.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can we take our break now and then resume after the envisaged time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I am a little bit surprised. It is really very early for the second break. Usually we have our second break half past 12.00, not quarter before 12.00. You gave us as a reason that the witness might be tired, but after 50 minutes there should be not reason for this. You want to interrogate him for nine hours all together and four hours by the Prosecution. You should use our time properly. It was just a question about a year and the fact of an arrest. I think you should continue a bit further. I don't see any sign of reason for an early break now. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let me go back to the question I put earlier on about medical evacuations. Mr. Kralj, do you know which were the months during which the medical evacuations you are aware of took place? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were medical evacuations by land and in cases of urgency by helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who organised these medical evacuations and who arranged for their transportation and who approved these medical evacuations, as needed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR took care of the transportation upon an approval issued by the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kralj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have document 05061 called up in e-court. Can we have it on our screens. We can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It's a letter from the Main Staff of the VRS, dated the 14th of February, 1995, and sent to the UNPROFOR command in Sarajevo to General Brinkman. It concerns one of the inspections as a result of which there was a medical evacuations. I will read what it says: "General, sir, today on the return of my team from Sokolac and upon completing the inspection of a helicopter mission during which one child was medically evacuated and accompanied by two members of the child's family, the chief charged with the inspection reported on the following: The planned and approved helicopter mission comprising one Arapaho helicopter took place without any problems or objections, just the way it had been approved in terms of the route, the timing of the flights, and the list of passengers. At 1130 hours, as the helicopter returned from Gorazde and landed on the field in Sokolac, the helicopter's motor was turned off in order for the inspection on the return to be effected. At that point in time, one could clearly hear the sound of yet another helicopter motor which was flying from the direction of Han Stjenica, some 10 kilometres south-east of Sokolac. This was something that the helicopter crew of UNPROFOR was also able to hear but failed to make any comments on. Members of the crew visibly showed great surprise at hearing that which could be clearly seen through their gesticulations." Mr. Kralj, did you ever take part in inspections, such as this one, of UNPROFOR helicopter missions just as the one that I've read about?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my role as a translator, I was in a position to be a part of the inspection team checking up on helicopters whose flights for Srebrenica or Gorazde had been okayed. On their arrival from Sarajevo, they would land at the football pitch belonging to the local football team in Sokolac. There were clear landing markings made on the pitch to facilitate the landing of helicopters. The inspection team checked the cargo carried by the helicopter, and my task was to check the passenger list and the identification or cards carried by the UNPROFOR members. In other words, I was supposed to make sure and check the identity of the persons involved. I was to check that they were indeed the persons they wish -- presented to be. The same procedure was repeated whenever they landed on -- on their arrival from Sarajevo and on their return from the mission before they proceeded to Sarajevo. I am familiar with this instant case because it was much talked of. It was said that the Muslim side had used the approved flight route to accomplish certain tasks of theirs and to fly over our territory in conditions of poor visibility all the way through to the territory under the control of the Federation, of what is Federation today, and was then Muslim controlled territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kralj. Since you were there, can you tell us if you, yourself, saw, or, rather, heard the sound of that other helicopter -- I'm sorry, it was your colleague who was there. Did he tell you if he had heard the sound of that other helicopter and was the conclusion -- was any sort of conclusion reached as to where this helicopter was headed, since you, yourself, said that it was much talked about, and whether this constituted a violation of the no-fly zone?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a no-fly zone, and the helicopter came from the protected zone and entered a Muslim territory in the direction of Sarajevo, according to the statements of the team leader who conducted the inspection and the report he submitted to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The witness has already answered the question. I was on my feet because it is -- first, it's a leading question. If he wants to know what this witness's colleague told him, he can simply ask him, What did the colleague tell you, if anything. The question was put in such a way that it suggested to the witness the answer or the substance of the conversation in question, so it's objectionable. Second thing is that it was a three-part question. There were three in one. I see that the witness found his way through it, but I would just bring that to the Trial Chamber's attention so that we are able to maintain a clear record for the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I apologise that I didn't see you earlier. That was my concern, too, and therefore I would like to put a question to the witness. Sir, do you recall that you said: "I am familiar with this instant case because it was much talked of. It was said that ...," and then you continue. That was what you said first. What was the source of your knowledge? Who did tell you this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The inspection team leader told me, Colonel Pandzic. He said that such things were happening and that I should also look out for sounds of other helicopters. In this specific case, when we conducted the inspection, I was able to identify General de Lapresle. I didn't know that he was a general, and I asked him for his ID. When I was suspicious, I also demanded that the person in question take off his helmet. Visibility was limited, and it was a kind of awkward situation because there was a bit of dismay at the fact that I did not know who General de Lapresle was. Colonel Pandzic was an expert for aviation and helicopters, and he identified the helicopter and explained me what the Muslim forces were doing to make use of these helicopter flights because they had helicopters available. One of these was to use the open corridor because we only had some make-shift anti-aircraft weapons that could harm helicopters. When the corridor was opened, that is the corridor through which the helicopter was allowed to fly, then nobody would use anti-aircraft weapons because the corridor had to be open, and they used that corridor while the inspection was being conducted on the ground to fly through. The innocence typically took about 15 minutes. I did not hear a helicopter fly over in this specific case, but it happened before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, after this answer, you will realise that you put quite a lot of details in your last question which was the concern of Mr. Vanderpuye. Try to avoid leading questions, please, and put open questions to the witness. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. I have no reason to ask leading questions. It just happened like -- inadvertently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since we are speaking about misuse of medical evacuation, can you say what these consisted in? Apart from this case you mentioned, do you know of any other instances and what was carried then if they weren't carrying wounded people?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
