utterances.text: As the persons transported were not thoroughly inspected, there was some information that they were transporting persons who are not UNPROFOR members but were dressed up as if they were, and they also carried UNPROFOR IDs. That's why there was an order for a qualified person who speaks languages to conduct an inspection and check all persons supposed to travel. Colonel Pandzic was in charge of helicopter flights and helicopter transportation to prevent anything from happening that was not announced or was not -- or could not be qualified as medical evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kralj. You have just spoken about some measures that had to be taken to make the corridor for medical evacuation safe. What was the side carrying out the medical evacuation, in this case UNPROFOR, supposed to do, and what was the VRS supposed to do with regard to UNPROFOR which was carrying out the medical evacuation by helicopters? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR was duty-bound to announce the evacuation to the Main Staff of the VRS in accordance with the -- with the genuine needs on the ground, and they were not subject to the limitations that applied to convoy movements and the movements of individuals. The Main Staff considered such instances of medical evacuation and they applied the urgent procedure in such cases. They would check what it was about and order the units to make sure that the route is safe. An inspection team would be formed and they would inform UNPROFOR command as soon as possible that the evacuation was approved. In principle, approval was given for all medical evacuations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us take a look at paragraph 2 of this document drafted by Mr. Djurdjic. It says, I quote: "In this case, it is clear that the corridor approved was used by the Muslims who were aware of the schedule of flights to conduct one more flight of the many flights that they had made. They abused the open corridor which we have informed you about a number of times before. We remind you once more that the Muslim forces are intensively using helicopters toward the enclaves and from the enclaves at night and in day-time when the corridors are open for UNPROFOR missions. In order to conceal that, you know that they are painting their helicopters white and marking their flags with the letters 'UN.' This conduct clearly shows inappropriate audacity on the part of the Muslims."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot follow because the page has been turned too soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have to go back to the first page. Mr. Tolimir, you stopped with the sentence: "This conduct shows inappropriate audacity on the part of the Muslims." Could you please continue from there on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I cannot read because ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we have the whole page back on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now we can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now this says, the last sentence reads: "And the powerlessness of the UNPROFOR forces to ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please turn the page, interpreter's remark.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "... to control the situation toward the enclaves and from the enclaves involving the bodies of the other side, too." Now, my question to you is: Do you know if the Muslims abused helicopter missions, medical missions, in previous or other instances as is stated here? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with the document, and Djurdjic and Pandzic who dealt with these issues also informed me that the Muslims on several occasions used approved UN flights. They need not have been about medical evacuation. It was the same with the flights from Srebrenica to Tuzla. The distance is very short and they used their own helicopters painted white with "UN" marked on their flags. There was such reports from the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said that they used UNPROFOR helicopters. Did they, in fact, use UNPROFOR helicopters in these dealings, or did they only use the corridors and the time slots given to UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR helicopters differ from the helicopters that the Muslims had, but the Muslims' helicopters were painted white, and they used UN symbols to trick the soldiers who had light anti-aircraft weapons capable of shooting down a helicopter. But, of course, there was a ban on shooting at UNPROFOR helicopter because UNPROFOR helicopters flew elsewhere towards the demarcation line between the Muslims and the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kralj. In this last section, the last two paragraphs, General Milovanovic speaks about possible disastrous consequences. Please explain to the Trial Chamber what is meant by that and why the general reacted the way he did to prevent those disastrous consequences from happening?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The worst case scenario was the accidental or deliberate shooting down of a helicopter marked "UN" and I'm -- and if this turns out to be a genuine UN helicopter because even if a UN helicopter was not announced or was flying anywhere near the demarcation line, the position was that such aircraft must not be shot at. There were reports about instances that, during a period when our representatives were present, fire was opened at UN helicopters but, fortunately, they were not shot down. They were hit but not shot down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell the Trial Chamber what reasons the Main Staff had for carrying out missions, such as medical evacuations, to be conducted mostly on the ground if the state the person or persons to be evacuated were in allowed that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The safety of UNPROFOR had to be guaranteed. It is much easier to secure a road than a flying helicopter. There was always the risk that someone might open fire, be it from the VRS side or by Muslim forces, and they -- we also wanted to prevent the Muslims from abusing the open corridor, especially in conditions of poor visibility and bad weather, so they wouldn't be able to fly from the enclaves to Tuzla or Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kralj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender document 05061.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 5061 shall be assigned Exhibit D335, marked for identification pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kralj, I would like to get a clarification from you. You said: "... during a period when our representatives were present, fire was opened at UN helicopters but, fortunately, they were not shot down." Who opened fire on UN helicopters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was an incident in Gornji Vakuf which was controlled by the Muslim Croat forces. Aboard a helicopter was an interpreter, Rade Kosic. Such incidents also took place once liaison officers began operating as well as during missions in the territories of some other units in the Federation. These things began happening when liaison officers were assigned to different staffs or corps to liaise between the sides. There was a mission in the territory of the 1st Krajina Corps, and Rade Kosic, the interpreter, was present. There I saw a Main Staff document containing a report about that incident. It was stated that fire was opened by the Muslim Croat side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could we next have 1D876. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see that this is a document of the Main Staff of the VRS. It was sent on the 28th of August, 1993, to the commands of units and corps of the VRS. We see a handwritten note. It reads: "Draft our specific order and sent to all units." We see some initials. Could you tell us whose initials they are and whose note it is?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was written by Zdravko Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did General Milovanovic send this order to all corps commands, as far as you know, as you were familiar with the structure of the VRS and because you also sent documents to the corps commands?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We see that it was an urgent document which means it had priority over other documents as to when it would be sent out. It was addressed to all corps commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at the introduction of this document just following the list of addressees: "Based on an appraisal of the situation at check-points and security at bridges by the organs of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska for the purpose of fully functional inspections at check-points and security of bridges, I hereby order: "1. Check-points must function continuously, 24 hours a day. Take urgent measures in this regard. "2. Check-points at which inspections of humanitarian aid convoys and UNPROFOR are carried out shall be exemplary. Select the men for the job, equip and dress them in the M-89 uniform, and train them to inspect convoys in a well-mannered and professional fashion. Be very correct and dignified when communicating with UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations. Place check-points where there are facilities for freshening up, eating, and overnight stays when necessary; be hospitable towards UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations. Of course, they will pay for the satisfaction." My question is this: What were the requests of the Main Staff concerning the personnel at check-points towards the units which were supposed to man those check-points through which convoys passed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, the document was sent from the Main Staff. At the time, I was in the 1st Krajina Corps. I was their liaison officer. The document was received by the operational department as an order. The corps commander, pursuant to item 2 of this document, issued his order in turn to the Gradiska Brigade which set up a check-point ordering them to abide by these instructions starting with the selection of personnel, securing conditions for unhindered stops of the convoys so as not to disrupt the rest of the traffic. They also needed to find appropriate facilities where members of the convoy or UNPROFOR could meet their basic needs or even stay overnight, if necessary. In the 1st Corps we did not have instances when they requested to stay overnight, but they did have to make use of our toilets and other facilities in case they had to stay there for some time. It was also required that the units provide adequate personnel. Many people thought that if a soldier was unfit to fight at the front lines he should be sent to a check-point, but once this order came in people were adequately trained, equipped, and prepared. They were given the best equipment. The best people were hand picked all in order to satisfy this order. My role as liaison officer was to inspect the check-point and draw up a short report as to whether the instructions were abided by. I was also authorised to instruct check-point personnel on how to address and communicate with the convoy members in an appropriate way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think it's now the time for the second break. We will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, since you mentioned a moment ago that you participated in the training of those who manned the check-points, did you train them in anything -- in anything in particular, or, in other words, can you tell us what your role was?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, if possible, we wanted to have people who could speak English. Second of all, they were supposed to be experts trained in working with metal detectors. We also looked for people who were familiar with the different types of goods or military equipment that could be found in such convoys. Basically, the team were mixed and experts were attached to those teams, from time to time, depending on the type of cargo. In other words, the personnel were qualified enough to perform an inspection in a quality, well-mannered way, be it an inspection of a convoy or of an individual vehicle at their check-point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could 1D876 be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D876 shall be assigned Exhibit D336. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please, it should remain on the screen for a moment because I would like to ask a question. Can we see the top of the page, please, again, and especially the handwritten note. Mr. Kralj, can you tell me, to whom was this order of Mr. Tolimir addressed in the handwritten note?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The handwritten remark referred to the person who was drafting the document to be submitted for signature. In the header -- or, actually, at the bottom of the document on the left-hand side we can see who the person was who did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand what you said. It was type-signed by Mr. Milovanovic, if I am not mistaken. Yes. Manojlo Milovanovic. Is the document from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska? And perhaps you can provide me with some information about the way this was done that was already in a written form and then with the handwritten note of Mr. Tolimir. What did he mean by "draft our specific order to all units"? To which unit? And what should be drafted that was already drafted, this document? I really don't understand that. Please help me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the very top of the document on the left-hand side, the header itself. This document was not registered or logged in the office of Colonel Djurdjic; in other words, it was done in -- in operational way which doesn't necessarily mean that Djurdjic could not provide certain input. It was obviously an operations order bearing the number of the operative worker and it is in the form of an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who drafted this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can't see that. It was customary that the operations organ drafted orders such as this one based on its number which is 02.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we scroll down a bit, please, to the bottom. Do you see any note who drafted that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't say who wrote the document. It is possible that General Milovanovic himself wrote it. What we see on the right-hand side is the code of the location whence it was sent, so it was an encrypted military line along which it was transmitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this stamp bears the date 31st of August, 1995, at 1150; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. It was sent out as a telegram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. At which point in time, if you know, did Mr. Tolimir receive this piece of paper where he put his handwriting on? Before that was sent out to the units or after? Can we see the top of the page again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tolimir could have added this note only to a document that was already finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is the reason why I ask. If that was already finished, it was drafted and perhaps already sent out to the subordinated units, what does it mean "draft our specific order to all units"? What did he mean by that? Which specific order should be drafted, by whom, and sent to which units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One can tell from the heading that certain units have been left out; namely, the airforce. Most probably Tolimir meant that an order should be drafted and sent to all units since the only ones included in this letter are the various corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is possible, but why did he say "draft our specific order ..." if that refers to this document, because that was already drafted and finalised according to what you just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is not self-explanatory in those terms. It doesn't really say why an additional document should be drafted, but it is possible that the purpose was to send it to others simply for their information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, to supplement the Presiding Judge's question, I'd like to ask you whether you remember a specific order that would have been sent by General Tolimir pursuant to this order and sent out, therefore, to all other units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this point in time, I was in the 1st Corps. I am only familiar with the part of this document which concerns the convoy, so I can't give you an answer that will be more precise than this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we show the document so that we can see both the top and the bottom stamps. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We just had it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, can you tell when this document was written in the Main Staff? It states so in the top left-hand corner. The VRS Main Staff, strictly confidential, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reads 30 August 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now look at the stamp that we have in the bottom right-hand corner. What date does it bear?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document was transmitted a day later, the 31st of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And you see three abbreviations, TLR, TGR, TLF. Do you know what they stand for? TLR?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Teleprinter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since this was transmitted by teleprinter a day after it was written, is it possible that this was a document originating from a lower level unit subordinated to the Main Staff? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at the handwritten note at the top of the page. Thank you. I am reading out what it says here in the handwriting: "Write or draft our specific order to all units." And a signature. This is my question: Do you know whose signature this is and does this come from the Main Staff or from some other quarters? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that it had come from a place other than the Main Staff because it's not really clear where the document was circulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the upper left-hand corner of the document, it says the VRS Main Staff. Does this denote who the order belongs to or who it was issued by?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an order of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the upper part of the document, above the initials, it says "write our order" or "draw up our order." This is my question: Could someone who had this Main Staff order have wanted to produce, based on this, an order of his own?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you give us your opinion as to whose -- who this signature might belong to? Have you ever seen it before?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, some minutes ago you said it is the handwriting of Mr. Tolimir and his signature, without any reservation. Then I asked you about this handwriting of Mr. Tolimir. There was no doubt that this is from Mr. Tolimir. Why does it now so doubtful for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, because there's mixed Cyrillic and Latin script here. The note was written in the Cyrillic script and the signature, if it is in the Latin script, then it seems to be that "ZT," the first letter might be Z, but I am not clear on the signature at all. I will stand by my previous answer that I am not certain. I do believe it to be Tolimir's, but I am not one hundred per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At the beginning of your testimony about this document, you, without any reservation, said it is Mr. Tolimir's handwriting. The handwriting and the signature haven't changed since then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom in a bit more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Here you go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On close examination, I am not sure this is Tolimir's signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I can't exclude that there is a translation issue. Could you please read the full text of the handwriting into the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Write our specific order to all units." In other words, somebody is ordering that the order be written for all the various units; whereas it was usually the role of Tolimir to propose something of the sort. That's why I was a bit puzzled by what I read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, we see the whole telegram now. This is my question: Had this been a telegram from the Main Staff, would it have born General Milovanovic's signature? I'm sorry. I formulated the question wrongly. Had this been a telegram written in the Main Staff, would it have been the obligation to type-sign General Milovanovic in order to indicate for the staff that this was, indeed, from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It had to have the stamp and the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Had this by chance been sent by teleprinter to one of the subordinated units, would it have born the signature of General Milovanovic at the teleprinting machine?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would have had to have the signature and the stamp of the teleprinter bearing the time when it was sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Had it been received by a unit outside of the Main Staff, and as it says here the date was the 31st of August, could the document have had the original signature affixed by General Milovanovic or would there only have been a type-signed name of General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please bear with me for a moment. You are now overlapping while speaking. Please avoid that so we have a clear record. Now it's your turn, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When a unit receives an order, the only thing the document indicates is what was typewritten; in other words, one cannot see either the signature or the stamp. And the teleprinter operator is duty-bound to place the date and time of its receipt and to forward it to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kralj. Please do not be upset by the fact that both the Judge and I are putting many questions to you on this document, but I know that this is a document that was written by the Main Staff, and I wouldn't object to placing my signature at the bottom of it when it comes to its content. The Judge's intention was to establish the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We both agree we try to find out the truth, but you should avoid to testify and to give facts, what you would have done. Indeed, we just want to understand the procedure what was in place at the relevant time in the Main Staff. Thank you very much. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can the document please be admitted -- oh, it's already been admitted. Yes, I have just seen my note to that effect. Can we now call up 1D876. Thank you. I'm sorry, my mistake. 1D1052. That's what I am seeking. Thank you. Thank you. I made a mistake because this document preceded the one we have just seen. We can see that this was a document of the Main Staff of the VRS, number -- I think the first digit is 0. 07/something dated 9 April 1993. The subject line reads: "Order to Control Humanitarian UNPROFOR Convoys." It was sent to the commands of the 1st Krajina Corps, the 2nd Krajina Corps, and so on, including the airforce and anti-aircraft defence of the Drina Corps. Could we please scroll down to see the signature block. It was signed by deputy commander Major-General Manojlo Milovanovic. And this document was sent to the units coded. Let us scroll back to the top, please. Thank you. It says order number so-and-so, dated 2 April 1993, issued by GS VRS: "Regulates the movement of humanitarian aid and UNPROFOR convoys across RS territory. Taking into consideration the behaviour and attitude of UNPROFOR and the humanitarian organisations, and with a view to taking efficient measures, I hereby issue the following order:" And item 1 reads: "Check-points must be in function 24 hours a day" -- I apologise, I read from the other order by mistake. This order, in fact, reads: "Examine separately every member of the group controlling humanitarian aid convoys and remove from the group all those who have compromised themselves by acquiring personal gain or in any other manner." And I'll now read out item 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, while you were a liaison officer of the 1st Corps, did you receive such orders and do you remember the first orders about the setting up of check-points in the zone of responsibility of your corps? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did receive such orders and we acted upon them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It says in the following item, which is also numbered as item, it should be item 2, actually: "Select a person known for his honesty, morale, and expertise and appoint him or her group leader." Thank you. Here is my question: Was an officer appointed to such duties at the time? Because you said that you were in charge of these check-points.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lower-ranking officer was appointed as a check-point commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, these two orders that we have seen, do they show that the Main Staff devoted some attention to check-points, and did the Main Staff do all that was necessary for them to function in accordance with the agreements reached in the central joint commission? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff took all measures necessary to have the check-points function in the best possible way. Firstly, by selecting personnel, their aspect and conduct with regard to UNPROFOR personnel or anybody else passing by these check-points. There were also analyses made and shortcomings were rectified.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look at item 4. It says: "In daily reports, provide data on humanitarian and UNPROFOR convoys which were checked or passed through your zone of responsibility." Here is my question. Was that dealt with in the daily combat reports the same way as any combat activity about which there was reporting daily? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a mandatory component of the combat reports, namely, the activities of UNPROFOR, no matter whether they passed or not. If they did, then the relevant information would have been included. If they didn't, then there was a remark saying that no UNPROFOR or humanitarian aid convoys passed today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you worked in the 1st Corps and in the Main Staff, tell us whether there were any incidents where people came to harm at these check-points?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no incidents in the territory of the 1st Krajina Corps, and later during my stay there were no major incidents at check-points either. There were some talks and verbal arguments, but no incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D1052 shall be assigned Exhibit D337. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, can you explain, since you were a participant in the events, what the difference was between UNPROFOR convoys and humanitarian aid convoys? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR convoys were armed. They had combat assets, personnel, or they supplied their units in the protected zones with the material; whereas humanitarian convoys were UNHCR convoys or International Committee of the Red Cross or Doctors Without Frontiers or other organisations that carried supplies for the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see Exhibit D303. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here is a document, Mr. Kralj, a document of the Main Staff as we see in the letterhead, Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. The first two digits of the number are 09, and it's dated 31 August 1994. It was to be dispatched to all commands of the corps mentioned there, and the subject line is: "Order Regarding Movement of Humanitarian Aid Across Lines of Separation." Thank you. Take a look at the end of the document and you will see the signature of deputy commander General Manojlo Milovanovic. It seems we will have to turn the page to see the signature. You can see it now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go back to page 1 now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will now read the first paragraph. I quote: "You know that the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska no longer has any jurisdiction or responsibility concerning the approval of entry and movement of teams and convoys of organisations through the territory of Republika Srpska." Second paragraph: "This approval is now issued by the co-ordinating body for humanitarian aid and the Ministry of Health, Labour, and Social Welfare." Third paragraph: "The Army of the Republika Srpska has the obligation to check teams and convoys of humanitarian organisations passing through the territory of Republika Srpska and crossing lines of separation into territory controlled by Muslim and Croatian forces."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you shouldn't continue reading because the time for our today's hearing is over. If you have one question according to what you have just read, you may put this final question to the witness or you may want to continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here is my question to Mr. Kralj: To who did the Ministry of Health give approval? Do you know? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of Health gave approval to those who transported medical material. In a word, Doctors Without Frontiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. We will continue tomorrow with our questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Vanderpuye, do you want to raise something?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, only briefly, Mr. President. I just wanted to have an idea from General Tolimir approximately how much time he expects to use tomorrow, just so that I can prepare to start, if necessary, or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, what is your estimation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My estimate is that we will use as much time as planned, possibly a bit less, so that tomorrow after the first break we will be able to communicate to Mr. Vanderpuye if we are likely to finish before the time estimated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for the record, you have used in examination-in-chief, up to now, 5 hours and 38 minutes. You have an indication, Mr. Vanderpuye. There is a possibility that you may commence your cross-examination tomorrow. Sir, we conclude now our today's hearing. We will continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. Please be reminded that it is not permitted to have contact to either party during the break. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 25th day of January, 2012, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
